title: N.L.’s top-billing doctor faces malpractice lawsuits from 2 former patients
summary: The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador's top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely…

image.caption: Ophthalmologist Dr. Harry Dang, who billed MCP more than $4 million in each of the last two years, is facing malpractice lawsuits brought by two former patients in St. John’s, N.L. (Harry Dang/LinkedIn)

blocks.text: Nfld. & Labrador·New

The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador's top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely blinded during a botched cataract surgery.
Lawyer for Dr. Harry Dang says ophthalmologist will fight allegations

The ophthalmologist who was Newfoundland and Labrador top-billing doctor for the last two years straight is being sued by two former patients, including one who says his right eye was completely blinded during a botched cataract surgery.
The other ex-patient is accusing Dr. Harry Dang of performing a similar cataract procedure without taking into account an eye condition that rendered the surgery both futile and dangerous.
Dang, whose medical licence was suspended in December 2025 for unknown reasons, is rejecting the allegations, which haven’t been proven in court.

“We are defending these allegations and putting the plaintiffs to the required standard of proof,” said Dang’s lawyer Robin Cook in an email Wednesday declining an interview request on behalf of his client.

The College of Physicians and Surgeons of Newfoundland and Labrador is neither commenting on Dang’s suspension nor the lawsuits against him. The Jackman Eye Institute, where Dang worked until his suspension, also declined to comment.

items: N.L.'s top-billing doctor suspended by provincial regulator

blocks.text: The first suit against Dang was filed by St. John’s resident Lloyd Janes last June. Janes is also suing the Jackman clinic.
The Jackman Eye Institute on Newfoundland Drive in St. John's, N.L., on Nov. 13, 2026. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
According to a statement of claim filed in Supreme Court, during a cataract surgery in February 2025, Dang struck Janes’s right eye in an area with a high concentration of blood vessels.

Despite “diligent medical follow-up,” Janes “remains completely blind in his right eye and has been advised by medical care providers that this loss of vision is permanent,” reads the eight-page statement of claim, which adds that subsequent “corrective procedures” proved unsuccessful.

According to the same document, Janes’s left eye already had reduced vision and the surgery therefore had a significant effect on his mobility and health, making it “necessary to rely on family members and other individuals for daily assistance.”
Janes declined an interview request through his lawyer Ken Mahoney.
Second suit
The second former patient, Pierre Kusters, filed his own lawsuit against Dang earlier this fall, on Sept. 25.

Kusters’s statement of claim alleges he underwent a barrage of pre-surgery tests in June 2025, but was never informed of the results. His left eye was operated on two and a half months later. Ever since, he says his vision in that eye has been blurrier than it was before the cataract procedure, according to the document.

Pierre Kusters, a local cellist, underwent a cataract surgery performed by Dr. Harry Dang in September 2025. He says he can no longer drive at night and can no longer read most of his sheet music. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)

Kusters alleges three months after the surgery, and a few days after Dang’s licence was suspended, another ophthalmologist at the Jackman clinic told him the preliminary tests he underwent before the procedure showed he had a pre-existing degenerative eye condition called Fuchs dystrophy.

The disease affects the innermost layer of the cornea and makes cataract surgery ineffectual if the patient doesn’t also receive a cornea transplant at the same time, Kusters said in an interview with Radio-Canada.

"Dr. [Chris] Jackman confirmed that the finding was present in the tests and scans taken on June 25, 2025, prior to the plaintiff's cataract surgery. This was not known to the plaintiff and was not mentioned by the defendant in the pre-surgery consultation,” reads Kusters’s statement of claim. “Individuals with Fuchs dystrophy are not eligible for cataract surgery as they do not properly heal.”

“I’m a bit shaken by it all,” said Kusters, a cellist with the Newfoundland Symphony Orchestra who can no longer read most of his sheet music. He said since the surgery, he can no longer drive at night and moved from Conception Bay South to Mount Pearl in the last month in order to have access to public transit.
Dr. Harry Dang hasn’t practised at the Jackman Eye Clinic since December 2025, when his licence was suspended. (Patrick Butler/Radio-Canada)
Like Janes, Kusters’s vision in his other eye is very weak. He is now waiting for two cornea transplants, a procedure for which there is a five-year waitlist in Newfoundland and Labrador.

“I’d would have liked to have known from the beginning, back in September 2025, that I had this disease. I’d been on a waitlist and maybe today I’d already have been operated on,” said Kusters, who is currently trying to book a surgery in Nova Scotia, where the waitlist for cornea transplants is significantly shorter.

“It’s like Alice in Wonderland. We’ve gone down this rabbit hole and we don’t know how we got there,” said Kusters, who has also filed a formal complaint against Dang with the College of Physicians and Surgeons.
Matthew Head, the CEO of the Jackman clinic, said he couldn’t provide “patient-specific commentary.”
“This matter is still with the legal and regulatory bodies,” Head wrote in an email on Nov. 8.
Dang billed $4M to MCP in each of last 2 years
In 2024-25 and again in 2025-26, despite his suspension with nearly four months left in the fiscal year, Dang was Newfoundland and Labrador’s top-billing doctor.
In 2025-26, he billed $4.25 million to MCP. The year prior, $4.91 million.

In an email Thursday, Donna Walsh of the College of Physicians and Surgeons wrote the organization was unable to comment on any physician or complaint “to ensure that any investigation and/or subsequent hearing is conducted in a fair and impartial manner.”
The regulator wouldn’t say whether Dang’s suspension beyond its current expiration date of Jan. 14, when all annual licences to practice medicine expire and must be renewed.
Dang has not filed a statement of defence in either action. The Jackman clinic also hasn’t filed a statement of defence in the Janes' suit.
